"I could," Clara said slowly. "As the honest part. The limit of the argument."

"You'll lose points."

"I might lose the debate and keep the truth. That's allowed. Mr. Nowak says the best debaters know where the text stops talking."

That evening Clara called Malaya and read her the 1966 facts, and Malaya responded with six texts, an eggplant emoji, and the revelation that her parish's Friday food drive was, as far as anyone could tell, exactly the kind of works of charity the old document had in mind, which meant Malaya's family and Clara's grandmother had been obeying the same rule in opposite costumes for Clara's entire life. "We're penance twins," Malaya texted. "This is the worst club I've ever joined."

At dinner the fish was excellent, and the walnut loaf, which Grandma finally admitted had stood in for meatloaf on more Fridays than she would confess to, was even better. Clara pushed her notes aside and ate. On Monday she would stand up in class and argue that the rule applied and did not apply, that it had been transformed rather than broken, and that what stayed uncertain, what no document could settle, was whether a practice done for love still counted as penance or had become something else entirely.

"Second helping?" Grandma asked, already lifting the plate.

"Works of charity," Clara said, and held out her fork.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The skate park behind the recycling depot had two good hours of light left, and Eli had a worksheet due Monday that he was determined to finish under them. He sat on the flat bottom of the quarter pipe with his back against the transition, workbook on his knees, while Luka carved wide lazy circles above him and Clayton lay along the coping like something the tide had left.

The problem was a plate one. Two parallel plates, charged up, some poor imaginary charge stuck between them, and the question asking for the field strength. Eli read it three times, wrote down the numbers, and divided. Fifty volts per metre. It looked clean. Clean answers had betrayed him before.

In March he had sat a physics exam with exactly this kind of question and walked out feeling fine, even pleased, the way you feel fine stepping off a curb you didn't know was there. When the paper came back, a whole question carried a red line through it, no marks, no comment, as if the marker had simply refused to discuss the matter further. His father had said maybe physics wasn't his subject. His mother had said maybe the marker was having a day. Neither had said the thing that mattered, which was that Eli had missed a retake by two points and now sat in a summer class with a worksheet and a bruise on his confidence the size of a small steppe, flat and wide and hard to cross.

Luka rolled down and stopped beside him, sneakers dragging. "What are you doing here, of all places?"

"Homework. Field between two plates." Eli angled the workbook. "You stick a hundred volts across them, they're two centimetres apart, and the field comes out fifty volts per metre. Done. One more question and I'm free."

Luka squinted at the page. Luka's relationship with physics was cordial but distant, like a neighbour you wave at. He pointed at the ramps, the fence, the flat grey concrete stretching to the fence line. "You ever think about how this park would measure if you did it in centimetres?"

"All the time," Eli said. "It's my hobby."

"No, I mean the whole park. Everything tiny numbers." Luka shrugged, as though he'd adumbrated some large idea and preferred not to say it outright. He pushed off and went back to carving.

Eli looked at his fifty. It had the inchoate rightness of an answer that had not yet been checked, which is to say it was a feeling, not a fact. He measured the quarter pipe with his eyes. Two centimetres. Two centimetres was the width of two fingers. It was nothing. It was a gap you couldn't even fit a deck through. And a hundred volts across that nothing was supposed to make a field of fifty volts per metre, which meant that one metre of that field would only eat fifty volts, which meant you'd need two whole metres of the gap to account for the hundred volts he'd already put across two centimetres, and somewhere in there the arithmetic started to cough politely and look at the floor.

He flipped back through his notes. Summer class notes were different from school-year notes; they were desperate, honest things. Somewhere near the front, in the margin, in his own handwriting, was a box drawn around the words convert first. Below it, an example he'd copied without understanding in June and now, in the flat bottom of a skate park in August, understood completely: two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them. Two centimetres was 0.02 metres. The same problem. His fifty was a hundred times too small, and it had been a hundred times too small in March too, and nobody had told him, they had just drawn a red line and moved on.

"Clayton," he said. "You awake?"

Clayton opened one eye. "Barely."

"If I've got plates 0.02 metres apart and 100 volts across them, what's the field?"

"Five thousand volts per metre," Clayton said, without lifting his head off the coping, and closed the eye again.

Eli stared at him. "You don't take physics."

"My dad fixes medical equipment. He says it about the plates in the machines, says it like a lullaby." Clayton resettled himself on the concrete. "Two centimetres, a hundred volts, five thousand volts per metre. You want it in a minor key, I can do that too."

There it was. Eli wrote the number in the box, then sat looking at it, at the twin of the question he'd failed, solved on the flat bottom of a quarter pipe with one friend who couldn't do it and one friend who could do it without knowing how he knew. The old way of thinking, the March way, had been to trust whatever came out of the calculator and hand it up like an offering. The new way, he decided, was to trust nothing until you could hold the numbers up against something real, against fingers and gaps and the width of a kerb you didn't know was there. Whether that was wisdom or just a superstition with better manners, he honestly couldn't say. Some of it would stay unclear until the retake in September, and possibly forever, in the way that the true reasons you fall off things tend to stay unclear even after you get up.

He closed the workbook and stood, and the concrete gave his knees back their shape. Above him Luka carved another slow arc against the sky, and Eli picked up his board and dropped it on the flat bottom, wheels rattling once before they went quiet and true.

"You getting on the board," Luka called down, "or measuring it in centimetres?"

Eli pushed off.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: If a Java class defines no constructor, the compiler adds a default no-argument one; once you write any constructor, that default is no longer added.
story:
The queue for registration at the regional robotics competition stretched past the gym doors, and Carter shifted his toolbag from one shoulder to the other while Aariz held their place in line. Their robot was checked and ready, which left Carter with ninety minutes of nothing before the inspection slot, and a laptop in his bag with a half-finished assignment for Mr. Mensah's class due at midnight.

He found a folding table near the concessions and opened the laptop. The task was simple enough on paper: take the Robot class he had written last week, which held only private fields and getter methods, and add a constructor that took parameters so a robot could be created with its name and battery level already set. Then write a test for it. He had already written three tests the night before, and they had all passed, which was the kind of good news that made him suspicious.

He typed the constructor in, saved, and ran the tests. Two passed. The third, the one that created a Robot with no arguments and checked that its default battery read one hundred, failed with a message he read twice. No constructor taking zero arguments. He sat back and looked at the ceiling of the gym, where a banner from a sponsor two years out of date hung crooked over the far hoop.

He had not deleted anything. He had only added code, and yet something that used to exist, a constructor he had never written and never seen, was gone. He scrolled up through the file. It had worked the night before, when the class had no constructor of its own at all. Somewhere in that difference was the whole problem, and no one had handed him the rule, so he built it backwards from the evidence like a debugging problem: the class with no constructor could still be constructed with no arguments, and the class with one constructor could not.

Miles dropped into the chair across from him with a paper boat of fries. "You look like your code died."

"Worse. My code lived fine until I improved it." Carter turned the screen toward him. "Watch." He commented out the new constructor, ran the test, and it passed. He uncommented it, and the test failed again. Miles chewed and watched the sequence twice.

"So before you wrote any constructor, one was being handed to you for free," Miles said. "And the second you write one, the free one goes away."

"That's the only thing that fits." Carter wrote a line in the margin of his notes, the plain statement of it, and underlined nothing because underlining was the kind of habit that pretended certainty. He fixed the test by creating the robot with arguments instead, which felt less like a fix and more like a decision about what the class owed him. He was honest enough to admit he did not know whether the old test had been wrong or merely obsolete; both readings were possible, and the compiler did not care which he chose.

The loudspeaker crackled through an interminable reading of inspection rules, and Aariz appeared at the table, still holding the team badge. "They moved us up. Table four, ten minutes."

Carter closed the laptop without shutting it down, letting the tests rest in their new state. On the walk across the gym he thought about how the whole morning underpinned something Mr. Mensah kept saying about code, that a system holds together only as long as its unwritten parts stay unwritten, though Mr. Mensah had never put it that way and neither, out loud, would he. At table four a judge in a grey polo asked for their autonomous run, and Aariz set the robot on the tape while Carter knelt with the battery pack, an ascetic arrangement of wires and zip ties, everything exposed, nothing decorative, and pressed the start button with the side of his thumb.

"Thirty seconds," the judge said.

"Then let's see what we built," Aariz said, and the robot rolled forward off the mark.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
The desk chair in her grandmother's front room still had the plastic sleeve on its cushion, and Rosalie sat in it the way she imagined a person with a job would sit, spine straight, hands folded, chin level. Across from her, Darwin held a printed page of interview questions he'd found online and read them in a voice he clearly thought sounded like a manager. "Tell me about a time you overcame a challenge." Rosalie met his eyes and held them, counting silently to four, because she'd read that four seconds read as confidence and five read as something else.

"Enunciate," Darwin said. "You swallowed the second half of that sentence." He was right, and she knew he was right, and she said the sentence again anyway, slower, letting each word finish. The room smelled of her grandmother's coffee and the lemon polish she used on the windowsills, and through the open door came the sound of Maxym pacing the hallway with his phone against his ear.

Maxym came in holding the phone out like evidence. "So the deli wants me Sunday," he said. "But Mr. Halloran put me on the slicer for the whole shift. Someone at school said that's illegal if you're seventeen. Someone else said it's only illegal if you're fifteen. Nobody actually knows anything." He dropped onto the ottoman. "I can't just quit, and I can't just say no if it's allowed, because then I look lazy."

Rosalie took the phone, typed, and read while the others argued about whether a sixteen-year-old could work past midnight. The federal page was plainer than she expected. "Here," she said. "Sixteen and seventeen year olds can work as many hours as they want, no limit at all. But the Department of Labor has a list of jobs it's declared hazardous, and that kind of worker can't be put in them." She scrolled. "Meat slicers are on the hazardous list for minors. You can close on school nights, apparently, but you can't slice the roast beef."

"Wait, so the hours thing and the machine thing are separate rules," Maxym said. "Both true at once."

"That's what it says." She turned the phone so he could see the page himself, because she'd learned from Darwin that people believed sources more than they believed friends. Maxym read it twice, then photographed it with his own phone, the shutter sound loud in the quiet room.

The next morning her grandmother's neighbor, Ms. Santos-Reyes, knocked at the door with a plate of guava pastries and stayed to help, or to supervise, it was never entirely clear which. She had interviewed people for thirty years at a hospital and had opinions. "Eye contact is not staring," she told Rosalie over the kitchen table. "It's returning. The manager looks away, you may look away. What you cannot do is apologize for existing." Her grandmother laughed at that from the stove and said the whole process had become capricious since her day, when you walked in, shook a hand, and started Monday. Rosalie asked Darwin, who was going through a philosophy phase before college started, whether confidence was a real thing or just a performance. "That's ontology," he said. "Whether a thing exists at all. I'd say it exists if it changes what happens." She wrote that on the back of her question page, then crossed it out, embarrassed by her own handwriting.

At the deli on Thursday, Mr. Halloran read her application without looking up, which undid half her practice in the first ten seconds. She answered his questions about school and availability in the clear, finished sentences she'd rehearsed, and when he asked if she had questions, she heard herself ask, in a voice steadier than she felt, about the slicer, and whether the schedule respected the rules for the younger workers. He set down the pen. "You the one who told Maxym about the hazardous list?" She admitted she was, and prepared to be told the position had gone to someone less interested in federal code. Instead he leaned back. "Nobody's ever asked me that. Fine. Sunday he'll be on register and cleaning, no slicing."

He slid a form across the counter for her, and it was only while signing that she did the arithmetic she'd somehow avoided all week. She was eighteen. Every hour restriction, every machine restriction, everything she'd studied until midnight at her grandmother's table, applied to everyone but her. "You start Saturday," Mr. Halloran said. "You'll train on the slicer first, since Maxym can't touch it." Behind him, the machine stood gleaming on its stainless counter, the blade she had spent a week defending her friend from, waiting and perfectly legal, for her.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Elijah had the clipboard in his teeth while he stacked cones on the pool deck, because the dive team had left the whole shallow end looking like a garage sale. Ms. Russo, who ran the community pool and had agreed, with visible reservations, to let him coach the twelve-and-under water polo squad, watched him from the office door.

"They can't pass," she said. "You told me that three times this week."

"I'm fixing it," he said, around the clipboard.

He had played since he was nine, and the problem was obvious to him the way a draft under a door is obvious to the person sitting near it. The kids threw the ball at their teammates' faces, or into the empty water two meters wide of them, and then looked at their own hands afterward as if the hands had betrayed them. Last season Elijah's own coach had been a yeller, a man who narrated bodies constantly: bend the wrist, extend the arm, snap the hips. Elijah had obediently bent his wrist for two years. His passing had been, in the technical vocabulary of his friend Zoe, "a war crime."

Zoe was stretched on the deck in her lifeguard chair, reading something for summer homework, and she called down to him now without lowering the book. "What's the plan, Coach? Are you going to pathologize their wrists one at a time, like our guy did?"

"Shut up," Elijah said, without heat. He liked Zoe precisely because she said things like that. "That's actually the thing I'm not doing."

The thing he was doing had come out of a frustrating night in July. He'd been drilling the kids on body mechanics, calling out corrections, and their passing had gotten worse, or at least no better, which at nine in the morning in a chlorinated room felt worse. That night he'd gone looking through a coaching forum, half-finished, and found himself reading about work by a researcher named Gabriele Wulf. The finding sat in his head like a stone in a shoe: learners usually improve faster when they're told to focus on the effect of a movement, on the target, instead of on their own body parts. He read it again. It was almost insultingly simple, and it also, he realized, explained two years of his own obedient wrists. He had spent his early teens staring inward at himself, at the machinery, and nobody had ever once told him to look at where the ball should go.

So this morning he had written, in his worst handwriting, a single instruction for every drill: hit your teammate's hands.

Kimberly, who played point and considered herself, with some justification, the best passer on the squad, was the first to object. "You're not telling us what to do with our arms," she said, treading water with the wounded dignity of a person who has been promised technique.

"Hit his hands," Elijah said, and pointed at the tall boy, Daniel, holding them up.

She hit his hands. It was a decent pass, flat and quick, and she looked as surprised as anyone. The tall boy threw back to her, and it sailed over her shoulder, and Elijah called out, "Kimberly's hands," and the next one arrived. The line moved. Zoe, above them, kept score of completed passes per minute, which she insisted on calling throughput, because she thought it was funny, and by the end of forty minutes the number had climbed from eight to twenty-one. Nobody had been told a single thing about their elbows.

There was a cost, though, and Elijah noticed it at the water station during the break. A small kid named Ben, who had the worst pass on the team and knew it, was doing better today and still looked miserable. "I still don't know what I'm doing wrong," Ben said. "Like, what my arm's even doing."

Elijah opened his mouth, and then closed it, because he had an answer and the answer was a hypothesis. He believed in the Wulf finding the way you believe in a rope you have just been pulled up with, but Ben was standing in front of him wanting something the rope didn't give: an understanding of himself, not just of the ball. Maybe those were different wants. Maybe, eventually, a player needed both, the outside eye and the inside one, and the order mattered, and the timing mattered, and he was seventeen and had no idea. He had been on the receiving end of a coach who pathologized every joint, and he had decided tonight that too much of that was gratuitous cruelty dressed as rigor, and he had not decided where the line was.

"You're doing fewer things wrong than yesterday," Elijah said. "Watch the ball into Kimberly's hands. Just that."

Ben nodded, unconvinced, and pushed off the wall toward the shallow end, where the others were already spread out, waiting, water slapping against the gutters. Kimberly spun the ball on one finger, then dropped it, then picked it up.

"Hit my hands," she called across the pool, and grinned at him.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
story:
The laptop took three minutes to load the map of her city, and Olivia spent those minutes watching her mother's mercurial mood move through the kitchen, bright over the dishes, dark again at the mail on the counter. The letter from the landlord had come that morning, the third notice about the basement apartment they had lived in since Olivia was nine. "Not now," her mother said, without turning around, when Olivia asked what it meant.

The assignment had come from Ms. Grant's seminar in the spring, before graduation: find a question your city could not answer about itself, and answer it. Olivia had thought she was done until she read the landlord's letter, and then the question assembled itself in her head the way the software assembled its layers, one transparent sheet over another. She opened the floodplain shapefile first, then the parcel data, then the census blocks, and let the program draw them together.

Jaylen had sent her a message that afternoon, part encouragement, part argument, the way all their messages ran. "my cousin did this for toronto," he had written. "the cheap housing sits right on the flood zones. not a coincidence either, that's the part that makes me insane. overlay it and take a screen recording, you'll see it in like ten seconds." Below that he had pasted a link, and under the link, one more line: "also the whole thing was invented in canada. roger tomlinson built the first computerized GIS in the 1960s, the canada geographic information system. they call him the father of GIS. weird that our textbook never said his name." She read that twice. She had assumed the software was American, like most of the software she had ever opened, and the correction sat strangely in her, the way corrected facts always did, half embarrassment, half pleasure.

The map rendered. She turned on the housing layer and colored it by median rent, greens for cheap, reds for dear, and the floodplain in translucent blue beneath. Then she zoomed to her own street. The blue lay over her block like a hand resting there. The green sat almost entirely inside it. She zoomed out and the pattern held across the whole east side of the river, cheap block after cheap block, blue over green, blue over green, with a corridor of dry, expensive red climbing the hill away from the water.

Her mother came to stand behind her, drying her hands on a towel. "What is that?" she asked. Olivia explained it in plain words, which was harder than the technical ones, that the program drew two true things on top of each other, where the water would go in a hundred-year flood and where the rents were lowest. Her mother looked for a long time. Her stoicism was not silence exactly; it was a decision, made daily, about how much worry to let show. Olivia watched her make it now, and then watched it fail a little. "So the letter," her mother said. "The landlord wants us to sign something about flood insurance."

They sat together and read the letter properly. It did not exculpate him; if anything it confirmed what the map had already suggested, that he had known, that the clause about "tenant responsibility for water damage" was not boilerplate but foreknowledge, written out in advance for people whose only affordable option was the blue part of the map. Olivia felt her own anger arrive and tried, the way Ms. Grant had taught them, to hold it beside the other thing she felt, which was the strange excitement of seeing clearly. Both were true. She did not know yet which one ought to govern what she did next.

Rose-Marie called at nine, and Olivia read her Jaylen's message aloud, the part about Tomlinson, testing it against her own surprise. "So a country that measures everything about its land built the first tool for measuring land with computers," Rose-Marie said. "That checks out. What are you going to do with yours?" Olivia said she did not know. She had the overlay, she had the letter, she had a screenshot where their block showed green under blue, and she had a college orientation in August in a city three hours away. She could submit it to the city's open data portal. She could bring it to the tenant association, which met on Thursdays in the church basement. She could do both, or she could find that both asked more of her than a summer allowed.

She worked until nearly midnight, exporting the map at different zoom levels, labeling each one in the corner the way a real cartographer would, her name small and precise. Her mother had gone to bed. On the last export she zoomed all the way back into their street until she could see the outline of the building itself, the rectangle she had lived inside for nine years, green under blue. She printed it, set it on the kitchen counter facedown over the landlord's letter, and turned off the light.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A dot after a note adds half the note's value, so a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4 time.
story:
The garage smelled of cut grass and old paint, and Ms. Murphy had cleared a workbench for Brianna at the start of the summer, saying only that a piano ought to be played by someone. Now the middle of August stood open in the doorway behind her, and the assignment sheet lay flat on the music stand: sixteen bars, melody with chord changes, written in standard notation, due to the online course by Friday. Brianna had nine bars done and a problem she couldn't name.

She played the ninth bar and counted aloud, one-two-three-four, the way she'd done a thousand times in this room, and the bar closed early. Three beats, then silence where the fourth should have been. She tried the phrase again, slower, as if the missing beat were a coin that had rolled under something and might be found with patience. Still three. She wrote the rhythm on scrap paper: a half note and a quarter note, which should have filled the bar, except that she'd written a whole note somewhere she hadn't meant to, or the melody had shifted under her, capricious as weather, deciding it wanted different harmony than she'd planned.

Her phone buzzed on the bench. A message from Usman, who was taking the same course from his cousin's apartment across town: "How's yours coming? I finished mine in two days and it's boring. Wish I'd taken longer." She typed back with one hand while the other held the pencil: "Mine's coming too slowly to be boring. Bar nine is one beat short and I don't know what to fill it with. Everything I try sounds like a doorbell." A pause, then his reply: "Don't fill it. Make the long note longer." She stared at that. Make the long note longer. She looked at the half note sitting at the start of her bar, its empty head like a small window.

She remembered, dimly, a worksheet from weeks ago, dots after note heads, and she'd skimmed it because dots seemed like decoration, the kind of thing teachers add to make simple ideas look harder. But she dug the worksheet out of her folder now and found the example: a half note with a dot after it. She hummed the melody and held the half note past its usual length, and something clicked into place, arithmetic arriving before explanation. She said it out loud to the empty garage, testing it: "A dot after a note adds half the note's value. So a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4." She counted it against the bar. One-two-three, then the quarter note, and the bar closed exactly on four, complete for the first time all afternoon.

She added the dot with her pencil, a small dark point trailing the note head like a moon behind a planet, and played the whole nine bars through. The line had changed character. Where before the melody had hurried, charming but shallow, trying to beguile the listener with movement, now it lingered at the top of the phrase, and the chord under the long note had time to open. She sat back on the piano bench and felt the strangeness of it: the smallest mark she could make on the page had done more than anything else she'd written.

Susan arrived the next evening on her bike, helmet still on, because she'd wanted to see the garage piano ever since Brianna had texted her a photo of it. "Play me the one that was broken," Susan said, perching on an overturned bucket beside the lawnmower. Brianna played bar nine with the dotted half note and watched Susan's head tilt. "That's better," Susan said. "It sounds like it's deciding something." Brianna pointed at the dot on the manuscript. "That's the whole thing. One beat's worth of decision, in one period." Susan leaned in until her helmet nearly knocked the music stand. "So the dot's not just for looks." "Not just for looks," Brianna said. "Though it is a little for looks. Everything in notation is a little for looks."

They worked through the remaining bars together, Susan calling out chord options while Brianna tested them, and Brianna noticed that she was making choices differently than she had the week before. She'd started the summer trying to imitate the songs she loved, chasing their lineage back through her playlists, wanting her melody to sound descended from something already proven. Somewhere around bar twelve she stopped reaching backward. She let the melody sit where it wanted, even when it landed on notes she hadn't planned, even when the harmony underneath turned plain instead of clever. She wasn't sure that plain was better. She was only sure it was hers.

Ms. Murphy came out with two glasses of iced tea and stood in the doorway listening, not saying anything, her presence more like a window than a judge. When Brianna finished the sixteen bars, all of them, played straight through with the page still wet in places from erasures, Ms. Murphy set the tea down on the workbench. "That long one in the middle," she said. "Do that again." Brianna went back to bar nine, held the dotted half note for its full three beats, and let the quarter note fall after it. Ms. Murphy nodded once, the way people nod at things they recognize without being able to name.

Late that night Brianna sat in the garage alone, the door open to the dark, copying the final version onto fresh manuscript paper. She wrote to Usman before she started: "You were right about not filling the bar. Also I was wrong about dots." She thought about the two weeks behind her, how she'd believed the problem was a missing beat when the problem had been a note that needed to be longer, and she wondered how often that was true of other things, arguments with her mother, maybe, or the summer itself. She didn't have an answer. She had sixteen bars, a dot, and a Friday deadline.

The pencil moved across the staff, five lines at a time. When she reached bar nine she drew the half note, then lifted the pencil and held it above the page for a moment, considering the small dot to come. Then she set it down beside the note head, quick and light, and moved on to bar ten.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The number of moles in a sample equals its mass in grams divided by its molar mass in grams per mole.
story:
Mr. Pereira had set out the reagents before first period, and by the time Emily arrived the smell of the acid already hung in the room, sharp and faintly like vinegar gone wrong. The assignment on the board asked them to predict how much product would form from a given mass of reactant before they ran the reaction at the bench. Emily read it three times. She had baked two hundred grams of flour into loaves the night before, weighing everything on her mother's kitchen scale, and she had understood the flour, the water, the salt. The white crystals in the dish in front of her might as well have been ground off the igneous lump of rock that sat on the windowsill as a paperweight, something Mr. Pereira had brought back from a field trip years ago and never moved.

Israel slid onto the stool beside her and leaned over her worksheet. "You look like a pundit who just found out the election was rigged," he said. "It's arithmetic, not philosophy."

"It's not arithmetic," Emily said. "It's a language I don't speak." She had written the mass of the reactant at the top of the page and then stopped. At home, grams had meant something because she knew what two hundred grams of flour looked like in a bowl, how it behaved under her hands. Here, grams of one white powder were about as meaningful as grams of another white powder, which was to say not meaningful at all.

Yasmin, across the bench, was already writing numbers with the confidence of someone copying a phone number she had known for years. Emily watched her long enough that Yasmin looked up. "What," Yasmin said, not unkindly.

"How do you know what to divide," Emily asked. Yasmin turned her own worksheet so Emily could see it. There was the mass of the reactant, and under it a number Yasmin had pulled from the periodic table on the wall, and between them a division bar. "The molar mass," Yasmin said. "You divide by the molar mass." She tapped the paper twice and went back to her calculation, and that was the whole of her teaching.

Emily sat with it. The mass in grams of her sample, divided by the molar mass in grams per mole, gave her the moles. She said it to herself the way she might say a recipe: mass over molar mass, that's the moles. She thought of the flour again, two hundred grams on the scale, and understood suddenly that the kitchen scale had never been weighing flour for her at all. It had been weighing the same thing every time, an amount of substance, and the flour was only one costume that amount wore. On her paper she divided and got a small clean number, and from that number, through the balanced equation, she worked forward to the product.

Then Israel, who had finished first and had been narrating his own brilliance for five minutes, went quiet in a way that seemed to presage trouble. His answer was twice hers. "I multiplied," he admitted. "Mass times molar mass. More mass, more moles, that made sense to me." Emily looked at his figure and then at hers, and for a moment she doubted the whole analogy, the flour, everything. But the equation on the wall had coefficients, and if his number were right the product would weigh more than the reactants they had actually set out, which even she could see was absurd. "You've got grams of stuff turning into more grams of stuff out of nowhere," she said. Israel erased his line, divided instead, and got her answer exactly.

They ran the reaction. The product settled as a pale precipitate in the bottom of the flask, and Mr. Pereira came around with the scale and weighed each group's yield. Yasmin's was closest to prediction. Emily's was under by a little, and Israel's, which he carried to the front desk like a trophy, came in above every prediction on the bench, above the theoretical maximum, a result Mr. Pereira noted with one raised eyebrow and the observation that some flasks had been wet when weighed.

Walking out, Emily told Israel about the flour, two hundred grams, the molar mass of flour if such a thing even existed, the idea that her mother's scale had been doing chemistry her whole childhood. He said it was a stretch, that baking was cooking and this was science, and they argued it down the corridor until they reached the doors.

At home that evening her mother stood at the counter with the scale, frowning at a recipe that called for ingredients by grams and a cupboard that offered only cups and spoons. Emily took the scale from her, set the bowl on it, and zeroed it. "Weigh it," she said. "Mass in grams, divided by molar mass, that's your moles." Her mother stared at her. "It's flour, Emily, not a chemical." Emily was already measuring.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
Brayden had promised himself he would not spend the whole science fair in the physics hall, and he had broken that promise within eleven minutes. He stood now in front of a folding table where Yasmin had set up her homemade capacitor: two squares of aluminum foil stretched tight on frames, a hand-crank generator, a voltmeter, and a handwritten sign that said, in her blocky capitals, THE INVISIBLE PUSH. Between the two foil plates she had taped a ping-pong ball coated in conductive paint, hanging from a thread.

"It's the field," she said, cranking the generator in slow circles. "That's what moves it. Don't touch anything."

Brayden had come to the museum that afternoon mostly for the free admission and because his mother had said the apartment was too quiet for a boy who was supposed to be revising. He knew what a field was the way he knew what a mortgage was: a word adults used, a shape of something far away. But the ping-pong ball swung toward one plate, then, when Yasmin reversed the crank, swung toward the other, and something about the obedience of it unsettled him pleasantly, as if the air between the foil were a substance with opinions.

A judge came by with a clipboard, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, and asked Yasmin the question Brayden had been silently dreading on her behalf: "So how strong is this field of yours? Can you give me a number?" Yasmin, who could solder anything and explain nothing, looked at the ping-pong ball as if it might answer for her.

"Distance," Brayden heard himself say. "You'd need the distance, right? And the voltage." He did not know where the sentence had come from. He only knew that the two plates were like the two ends of something, and that strength should depend on how far apart those ends were. The judge wrote something down, which did not portend anything good or bad, merely that she was listening.

Yasmin measured the gap with a ruler, tongue between her teeth: nine centimeters. The voltmeter read four hundred fifty volts. Brayden turned the numbers over in his head the way he turned over a lock combination, half listening while Taya, arriving with a pretzel from the courtyard, said the hall lighting made everyone look like they were underwater, and was anyone else hungry. He was not hungry. He was dividing.

"It's the voltage divided by the distance," he said. "Between two parallel plates, the field strength is V over d. That's it. That's the whole thing." He said it with the specific doubt of someone who has just discovered something and cannot believe it was lying there in the open. Four hundred fifty divided by nine. Five thousand volts per meter, a number so large and so clean that he made Yasmin check the arithmetic twice, and then a third time on his phone.

The judge came back, and Yasmin said the words herself, pointing at the foil: "The electric field strength between the plates equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them." The judge nodded and moved on, and Yasmin turned to Brayden with the expression of someone recalculating a debt. "I spent two weeks building this and you got the important sentence in one afternoon. That's robbery. I demand remuneration." He offered her half the pretzel Taya had abandoned, which she accepted.

What Brayden kept turning over, on the bus home, was not the arithmetic. It was that he had believed, all through school, that physics was a turgid subject, all derivation and no weather, and here was a law you could feel in your eyes: the closer the plates or the greater the voltage, the stronger the invisible push. He had walked into the hall thinking explanations were things other people handed you, and walked out suspecting you could build them yourself out of two numbers and a ruler. Still, a question stayed with him, and he liked that it stayed: why dividing worked at all, what was actually traveling across that empty nine centimeters. He didn't know. He took out his notebook and wrote, under the heading FIELDS, the question and nothing else.

At his stop, a man was arguing with the fare machine, slapping its screen as if the machine had a choice in the matter. Brayden watched the little spark jump when the man's sleeve brushed the metal edge, small and blue and gone. He stood there a moment longer, holding the door. "You feel that too?" he asked, mostly to himself. The man said nothing, and Brayden stepped down into the evening.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: On a lead sheet, chord symbols such as C, Am or G7 are written above the staff to show which chord accompanies each part of the melody.
story:
The church basement smelled of damp carpet and old coffee, and the radiator clanked in the corner like a metronome nobody had asked for. Jack sat at the folding table with his staff paper, a pencil, and a half-finished melody that had been half-finished for eleven days. Sixteen bars. Ms. Cruz had been clear about that: sixteen bars, with chord changes, written in standard notation, by Sunday, because the youth service needed something new and she was tired of the same three songs.

Ayesha came down the stairs two at a time, carrying her sheet music folder against her chest. She pulled a chair over, sat, and read his page upside down for a while before saying anything.

"It's pretty," she said. "The melody. But I can't play it with you."

"Why not? You're the pianist."

She turned the paper toward herself. "Because there's nothing here telling me what to do with my left hand. It's just the tune. If I'm going to accompany you, I need the chords. You write them in above the melody, where I can see what goes with what. That's how a lead sheet works. Chord symbols above the staff, each one over the part of the tune it belongs to."

Jack looked at his bars. He had C in his head for the opening, then something sadder for the fifth bar, the place where the melody dropped. He knew the sound he wanted but not its name. He wrote C above the first bar, and it looked strange up there, floating over the notes like weather.

Ayesha went upstairs to practise with the choir, and he stayed. The room was an ascetic little space, one bare bulb, a wall clock, a poster of the sanctuary from 1974, and he found the quiet useful. He played his melody on the battered upright in the corner, one bar at a time, and after each bar he tried chords until one stopped fighting the tune. The fourth bar wanted something with a seventh in it, unsettled, leaning forward. He wrote G7 and felt clever, then immediately unsure, because the melody note underneath clashed and he could not tell whether the clash was a mistake or the best thing on the page.

He thought about his uncle, who played bass and said once that chords were the ocean and the melody was the boat, and about Ms. Cruz, who had said the opposite in the spring: that the melody leads and the harmony follows, and a composer who forgets that writes accompaniment with a tune bolted on. Both of them had played for thirty years. Both of them were certain. Jack sat between the two ideas with his pencil hovering, and decided the honest thing was that he did not fully believe either one, at least not tonight, not for these sixteen bars. The chords were pushing the melody in places, and the melody was dragging the chords in others, and maybe that was not a problem to solve but the actual condition of the piece.

The radiator stopped. Outside, thunder had been building all evening, and the air through the window screen felt ionized, sharp and heavy, the way it does just before rain actually starts falling.

Ayesha came back down with two cups of water and stood behind him while he played the whole thing through. At the ninth bar, where he had written Am, she set her cup on the table.

"There," she said. "That one's the heart of it."

"You think?"

"I think it's the first place you stopped trying to be correct."

He played the ninth bar again, then the tenth, where the melody climbed back up over a plain C. On the page, his chord symbols sat above the staff in his careful pencil letters, C and Am and G7 and C again, each one marking what belonged where, and under them his tune ran on in black notes, and neither row looked like it was in charge.

Ms. Cruz appeared at the bottom of the stairs with the new hymnal under her arm, the one with the simplified choruses that she called populist and the older members called a disgrace. She looked over Jack's shoulder for a long moment.

"You'll play it Sunday," she said. "Both of you. Ayesha, take the chords as written, first time through."

Ayesha nodded and lifted the piano lid. Jack positioned his page on the music stand and squared it against the edge.

"From the top," he said, and set his pencil down on the table.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
Amy had claimed the card table in the corner of her grandmother's sunroom, where the windows on three sides made her feel like a specimen under glass. Her laptop, her grandmother's old dictionary, and a shoebox of photocopies from the town library formed a wall around her. The paper was due in two weeks, her first real research paper, with an argument about towns that tear down their old trees to widen roads, and she had chosen it partly because she could see the evidence from the window: the row of lindens on Maple Street, reduced that summer to stumps.

Her grandmother moved through the room watering plants, offering commentary. "When I wrote my thesis, we typed citations on index cards and lost half of them." Amy liked this. It made the whole strange ceremony of scholarship feel like something people had survived before her, like sewing or canning.

The hard part was not the reading. The hard part was the shape. She had eight sources: a book about urban planning, a newspaper editorial from 1974 defending the lindens, a journal article on street trees and cooling, a city council transcript, two more articles she had found through the library database, and a pamphlet from the arborist who had inspected the stumps. She understood, more or less, what a footnote did. It pointed, like a raised hand, back to whoever had said the thing first. What she did not understand was how the final list wanted to be arranged, and whether the arrangement was a rule or a courtesy, and who had decided.

She texted Rosie, who was doing the same assignment for the same teacher and had, Amy suspected, already finished it.

hey do sources in the bibliography go in the order you used them? like in the paper?

Rosie's reply came while Amy was cutting an apple at her grandmother's counter, and she read it standing in the kitchen light, juice on her thumb.

"no!! i did that and ms leblanc circled it. alphabetical by the author's last name, all of them. mla apa chicago, all the same that way. i had to redo mine last night. also your argument better not be that trees are nice, hers was, quote, a claim that could be wrong."

Amy sat back down at the card table and looked at her list, which ran in the proud order of discovery: the book first, because it had started everything, then the transcript, then the editorial. It was a diary of her own curiosity, and apparently it was wrong. She began sorting the entries by surname, and something odd happened. The 1974 editorial, whose author was named Aldous, floated to the top, ahead of the planning book she had read first. The paper's skeleton rearranged itself in her mind, the way a grove does when you walk into it from a different side. She had assumed the order of reading presaged the order of truth. It didn't, apparently. The list belonged to the sources, not to her.

The argument was harder. The editorial called the city's reasoning sophistry, paving over the shade that had taken fifty years to grow, and Amy had underlined it twice and then, later, felt embarrassed by the underlining. The council's side was not nothing. The road was genuinely unsafe at the corner; two accidents in three years. She drafted a page arguing that the trees should be replanted on the widened boulevard, medians wide enough for roots, and then read it and heard Ms. Leblanc's imaginary pen tap. Could a linden on a median survive road salt? She didn't know. She wrote in the margin, check, and left it, the uncertainty sitting in the paper like a knot in good wood.

Her grandmother paused behind her, reading over her shoulder the way grandmothers do, uninvited and welcome. "What's this word, bibliography?"

"It's the list of everybody I borrowed from," Amy said. "Alphabetical, apparently. Not the order I used them."

"Like a guest book," her grandmother said, "arranged by name instead of by arrival." She seemed pleased by this, and went back to her plants.

On Sunday Amy walked Maple Street with Leonard, who had grown up two houses from the stumps and remembered climbing the lowest branch of the third linden. He argued the whole way that memory counted as evidence, and Amy argued back that it didn't count in a paper, not without a footnote, and then wondered, saying it aloud, whether a person could ever really footnote the thing a street used to feel like. They stood a while at the corner where the road bent. In the empty strip where the trees had been, someone had planted a sapling, skinny and staked, too small to shade anything yet. Leonard crouched and pressed the soil around its base with both hands.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
Gabrielle spread her economics notes across the small table in the food court, anchoring the corners with a tray of cold fries and Sally's chemistry textbook, which was so heavy it doubled as a paperweight. On Monday Mr. De Vries had assigned each of them a question to answer aloud at the front of the class, and hers was this: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She had read the chapter twice. She could recite it. But reciting and explaining, she was beginning to suspect, were different skills, the way knowing the words of a song was different from carrying the tune.

"Explain it to me," Sally said, uncapping a highlighter. "I know nothing. Treat me like I know nothing."

"Okay." Gabrielle turned her cup in a slow circle. "So inflation is prices going up. And the central bank is the bank that's in charge of money for the whole country, and it can raise interest rates, which is basically the price of borrowing money."

Sally waited, highlighter poised over a diagram of polymer chains. "And?"

"That's where I lose it. There's a chain of things that happen after the rate goes up, and I can hold the first link and the last link but the middle keeps slipping." Behind her, the mall's new decorative court rose toward a skylight, its arboreal arrangement of plastic ficus so convincing that two sparrows had moved in and were picking at a fallen pretzel among the leaves.

"Everything's chains," Sally said, tapping the diagram. "This whole chapter is monomers linking up into polymers. One little unit, then another, then suddenly it's a plastic bottle. Maybe your economy is the same. One household decides not to borrow, then another."

Gabrielle wrote that down. It wasn't economics, but it was a way of seeing it, and she needed ways of seeing it more than she needed another paragraph from the textbook. "When rates go up, loans cost more," she said slowly, testing each step like ice on a pond. "So people borrow less. So they spend less. So stores can't keep raising prices, because nobody's buying." She looked up. "Is that it? Is it really that short?"

"No idea," said Sally. "I'm in chemistry."

Aayan dropped into the third chair with an iced drink that immediately sweated all over Gabrielle's notes. He had Mr. De Vries last semester and still spoke of him the way people speak of a coach who benched them and then won the championship. "He'll ask a follow-up," Aayan said, blotting the page with a napkin. "Something like, have central banks always done this, or did someone start it. He loves who-started-it questions."

Gabrielle had no answer for that. The textbook didn't either; it treated the target like weather, something that had always simply been there. While Sally ran to the phone store to check on a repair, Gabrielle wandered to the bookstore at the end of the corridor, past a rack of remaindered thrillers, to the economics section, three shelves of books with serious spines. Mr. De Vries himself was behind the counter, in his weekend capacity, and she felt an odd embarrassment at being seen studying on a Saturday, as though he had caught her practicing a private clumsiness.

She found it in a thin blue book with a cracked spine, and stood there in the aisle reading the page twice to be sure. When Sally came back with her repaired phone, Gabrielle was waiting by the arboreal court, the sparrows whirring up into the plastic leaves. "New Zealand," she said. "It was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting. The government and the Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent." She held up the page number. "So before that, nobody had written it down as a promise. Someone had to be first."

"That's your follow-up answer," Sally said.

"Maybe." Gabrielle folded the notes and put them in her bag. "The thing I still can't explain is why raising rates helps if it makes everything harder for people who borrowed money at the wrong time. Like it works, but it works by hurting." The court's speakers started a soft rain sound, fake weather for fake trees, and the sparrows settled again among the leaves.

That evening her mother asked how her Saturday had gone, and Gabrielle said fine, spent mostly at the mall, watching her grandmother, who was there to recuperate from her knee surgery, make three slow laps past the storefronts on her new cane. What she didn't say was that she had sat with her grandmother on a bench near the fountain and, when her grandmother asked what she was reading about, explained the whole thing, rates to borrowing to spending to prices, in ninety seconds, and that her grandmother had nodded and said, "So it's like a tap. Someone turns the tap, and the water slows." And Gabrielle had said yes, exactly like that, and then had thought, all the way home on the bus, that it wasn't exactly like that, that a tap was too clean for a thing that worked through mortgages and layoffs and decisions made in rooms she would never see.

On Monday she stood at the front of the class with her notes face down. Mr. De Vries listened, arms folded, and when she finished he asked the follow-up, and she gave him New Zealand, March 1990, 0 to 2 percent, and watched him write something in his book. "And the part you're unsure of?" he asked, because he always asked that, and she said, "Why hurting the borrowing slows the hurting of the prices, and whether that's a fair trade," and he didn't answer, just said, "Hold onto that one," and called the next name. She sat down beside Aayan, who slid over a folded note that said not bad, and she put it in her pocket with the page number still inked on her palm.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
The mailbox on Delmore Street had a dented baseball shape in its side, and Maelie's mother told her to pull up beside it, easy now, easy. The car behind them was closer than it should have been, a silver hatchback whose driver had been riding three feet off their bumper since the stop sign. Maelie's hands tightened on the wheel until her mother said, in the voice she used for airports and hospital waiting rooms, "Don't worry about him. Worry about what you're doing."

That was the trouble, though, deciding what she was doing. Her mother wanted her to count seconds at the car ahead, one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three, which felt excessive on a street where nobody drove faster than a lawn tractor. Laurianne had texted that morning: "btw two seconds is plenty, my cousin's a cop, three is for grandmas." Maelie had read it twice while eating toast and then left the phone face down on the counter, because choosing between her mother and Laurianne felt like choosing between two versions of being a person who drove.

They came around the curve by the Hendersons' hedge and there was the recycling truck, wide and slow, bottles shifting inside it like rain on a roof. Maelie was already counting, and at one-thousand-two the truck braked, and at one-thousand-two-point-something she braked too, hard enough that the seatbelt bit her collarbone and the phone in her mother's cupholder slid and thumped against the dash. Nobody hit anybody. The truck rolled on. Her mother looked at the windshield for a long moment.

"Three," her mother said. "Not two. Three, and you add a second for anything hard. Heavy traffic, rain, that truck. So this would be four." Maelie waited for the lecture, the part where driving became a metaphor for everything her mother thought she was careless about, but it didn't come. Her mother just adjusted the mirror and said, "Again. Find another car to follow."

So she found one, a blue sedan with a stick-figure family on the back window, and she counted. Three seconds when the street was empty and clear. Four when they passed the elementary school where crossing guards were setting out cones. Five, once, when a dog off its leash tore across the road and the sedan's brake lights bloomed red and Maelie was already slowing before they lit. Nobody honked. Nobody died. The counting stopped being her mother's rule and started being a rhythm, like the way she timed turns in the pool, and she understood, in a small quiet click, that Laurianne's two seconds wasn't wrong so much as a bet, and three was the same bet with room left for what she hadn't seen yet.

They parked in the church lot at the end of the street, and her mother let the engine idle and looked at her phone. "Text from Aaden," she said, and passed it over. Maelie read it: "You survived?? Mr. Martínez was asking if you'd be at the debate meeting Thursday. I told him yes. Also I told him you'd argue against his position, because honestly his whole 'driving culture commodifies freedom, sells it back to teenagers as a machine' thing is so cynical. He liked that, I think. He said, 'Good, then it will be a real debate.'"

Maelie laughed, an actual sound in the quiet car. Mr. Martínez had a way of making everything into a system, as if the suburbs were a theocracy whose god was the commute and Saturday night was its one hedonistic ritual. She didn't fully buy it. The wheel under her hands felt less like something sold to her and more like something earned, this morning, second by second. But she also didn't fully buy Aaden's dismissal, because two hours ago she had been the market's perfect customer, so hungry to drive that she'd have taken any rule from anyone with an answer. Maybe the truth was that wanting something badly made you easy to sell to, and the only defense was knowing what you'd actually paid. She texted back: "tell him yes for thursday and also that my counterargument involves the three second rule, he'll see."

"Ready to go back?" her mother asked. There was something careful in it, a door held open a crack, and Maelie understood that the whole morning had been this, her mother handing over something bigger than a steering wheel and not saying so.

"Can I drive the long way?" Maelie said. "Past the reservoir?"

Her mother fastened her seatbelt, and the click was the only answer, so Maelie checked the mirror, signalled, and pulled out of the lot counting under her breath, "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three."

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
The party had been going for an hour before Maelle found the privacy of the garage, where she stood in front of the mower with her phone held at arm's length like a mirror. "I'm available weekdays after four," she said to it, then broke off, because her eyes had drifted to the middle distance, exactly the way they had in Mr. Owusu's office on Thursday when he ran her through a practice interview and then said, gently, that she answered like someone apologizing for being in the room. She had gone home and decided to fix it before the real thing on Monday: the café on Fuller Street, fifteen hours a week, her own money at last.

She was still rehearsing when Kurt found her. He was voluble tonight, full of the party's momentum, and he leaned against the workbench and told her that Amos had eaten three slices of cake and was now trying to convince everyone to play sardines in the dark. Then he noticed what she was doing. "You're practicing for Fuller Street," he said. "You got the interview."

"I got the interview. I just don't know how to be in it."

That night, after the cake, she sat cross-legged on the garage floor while Kurt scrolled his phone on her behalf. "Okay, here," he said, holding the screen out. "In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements." He read it twice, savouring it. "So if the interviewer leans forward, you lean forward."

Maelle had a memory then, sharp and specific: she was nine, at her aunt's kitchen table, copying the way her aunt held her teacup, pinky out, because she wanted so badly to be liked by her. Her aunt had laughed and said, "You're turning into me," and Maelle had glowed for a whole day. Maybe it had never been magic; maybe it had been this. But something about it snagged. If the liking was something you could manufacture, then what exactly was being liked? She tried to introspect on this, sitting there with the mower and the smell of gasoline, and found she could not get to the bottom of it. She decided she would try it anyway, and decide what it meant after she had the job.

At the party's long table, Amos was holding court about the disbursement of the class trip fund, which had somehow arrived forty dollars short, and everyone was laughing at the word itself, which Amos pronounced like a legal verdict. Maelle used the table as her laboratory. When Amos crossed his arms, she crossed hers a beat later. When a girl near the punch bowl touched her collarbone while talking, Maelle touched her own. It worked, or seemed to: people turned toward her, leaned in, stayed. She felt a small cold thrill, and then a smaller shame, and then she stopped thinking about either because Amos was asking her a question directly and she had been so busy mirroring his posture that she had not heard a word of it.

"The trip," Amos said, patient, kind. "You were saying?"

She had been saying nothing. She had been performing saying. "Sorry," she said. "I was somewhere else." And he had leaned forward, so she had leaned forward, and the whole conversation had gone on without her in it.

On Monday the café owner turned out to be a woman who sat back in her chair with her arms loose in her lap, and Maelle, mindful of posture and movement, sat back too, arms loose, and answered every question with clear, direct sentences while some part of her watched the woman watch her. Twice the woman's eyebrows moved, faintly, and Maelle could not tell whether she had been caught or approved of. When it was over the woman walked her to the door and said, "You seemed relaxed for someone your age. We'll call you tonight."

That evening, at Amos's impromptu second celebration of nothing in particular, his birthday technically being over at midnight, Maelle was telling the table about the interview when her phone buzzed. She read the message twice. It was from the café, and it said: My co-manager sat in on your interview without you noticing, and she crossed her arms every time you did. We liked you. You're hired. Can you start Saturday? Maelle looked up. Amos was watching her face.

"What," he said. "Good news or bad news?"

"Both," she said, and showed him the screen.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, used a computer model called World3 to link population, food, industry, pollution and resources.
story:
The county water office smelled of damp cardboard and toner, and Alexis's desk was a folding table wedged between the filing cabinets and the window. Her internship was supposed to be data entry, twelve dollars an hour, but on her third morning the supervisor dropped a binder on her table and said the planning board wanted a model of how Fern Hollow's growth would affect its aquifer, something visual for the public hearing in August. Alexis had spent her senior year arguing with Anya about whether economics or ecology mattered more, a running debate that had survived graduation mostly through Anya's texts, and here, apparently, was the argument handed to her in a three-ring binder.

She started with the county's own numbers: wells, pumpage, projected subdivisions, a proposed bottling plant out past the highway. When she graphed them the lines crossed somewhere around 2031, which felt too tidy to be true, and she said so out loud to nobody. The woman at the next desk, who handled permits and kept an ascetic desk with a single pencil and a jar of instant coffee, looked over and said the old planning reports were in the basement, if she wanted to see how the town had guessed before.

In the basement Alexis found a 1994 report that had done almost the same exercise, and it had been wrong in ways she spent an evening untangling. The old modelers had assumed the bottling economy would grow forever, and had also assumed rainfall wouldn't change, and the two assumptions had cancelled each other into a straight line that history simply ignored. She texted Anya a photo of the crossed-out graph. Anya replied that it reminded her of something their civics teacher had mentioned senior year, a report from the seventies, and sent a link with the message: "World3. Population, food, industry, pollution, resources, all linked in one model. Read the actual thing before you argue with me about it."

Alexis read it at the kitchen table while her mother convalesced on the couch with a bad back and the television murmuring weather. The report was called The Limits to Growth, published in 1972 for the Club of Rome by an MIT team, and the model it used was called World3, and it linked population, food, industry, pollution and resources in a way that made her own little graph look like a child's drawing. She didn't agree with all of it; the global scale felt abstract compared to Fern Hollow's one aquifer. But the linking, the insistence that you couldn't move one line without the others moving, that she recognized. That was exactly what her graph had been failing to do.

The next day she rebuilt the model so the town's growth fed back into itself: more houses, more tax base, more pumps, a lower water table, higher pumping costs, fewer houses the county could afford to permit. When she showed it to Jayson, who was interning at the real estate office across the hall and had come by to steal the good stapler, he winced. "That's parasitism," he said, tapping her feedback loop. "The town feeding on its own water until it kills the host." She said that wasn't quite the word, growth wasn't an organism, and he said fine, but the shape was the same, and she wrote in the margin that the shape mattered more than the word.

At the hearing she stood at the front of the middle school cafeteria with her poster board and her laptop, and she gave them both versions. The county's version, which treated the aquifer as a number that declined smoothly, and hers, which treated the town as a system where everything touched everything, the way World3 had done for the whole planet in 1972. She mentioned the report once, briefly, a Club of Rome study out of MIT, and watched a man in a feed-store cap mouth the words to his wife. A woman from the bottling company's legal office said Alexis's model assumed the worst about rainfall, which was fair, and Alexis said the 1994 model had assumed the best and the truth had still been worse. She admitted, into the microphone, that she couldn't say which year the lines crossed, only that they crossed.

The board voted to table the bottling decision and fund a monitoring well, which everyone called a compromise and which meant, Anya texted that night, that nothing would change until the data came in, by which point the plant might already be permitted. Alexis sat on her floor reading the text over and over, trying to decide whether the evening had been a win. Her model might be wrong the way 1994 was wrong. The old report might be wrong too, or right in a way too large for one aquifer. She held both of them in her head the way she'd once held Anya's argument and her own, and found she could no longer fully separate them.

Her last day, the permit woman gave her the single pencil from the ascetic desk, sharpened to a stub. Alexis put it in her backpack with the basement report, which she'd asked to keep, and rode her bike past the field where the plant would go, or wouldn't, the alfalfa bent flat under a hard blue sky. At the edge of town she stopped where the pump station hummed behind its chain-link, took out her phone, and photographed the gauge on the main well, the needle steady in its glass, holding its place.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Upstage means away from the audience and downstage means toward it; the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience.
story:
The living room had been a stage for three days, and it was getting worse before it got better. Alexis had marked out the playing area with painter's tape, moved the couch against the wall, and told her mother that the coffee table was now "set dressing," a phrase her mother repeated at dinner in a tone Alexis chose to find affectionate. The one-act was thirty minutes long and had to be performance-ready in two weeks, which meant that tonight, finally, she had to stop talking about the play and start moving people through it.

Carina arrived first, script rolled in her fist like a baton. Jeffrey came ten minutes later with chips and an apology about traffic that nobody had asked for. They read through the first scene sitting on the floor, which went fine, and then Alexis said the word she had been saving up: "Okay. Blocking."

She walked them through it. Jeffrey would enter from the kitchen doorway, cross downstage, and sit on the taped-off bench. He got as far as the middle of the room before he stopped.

"Downstage is which way?"

"Toward me," Alexis said. She stood where the audience would be, at the edge of the carpet by the TV. "Toward the audience."

"That makes no sense. I'm walking toward you and it's called down?"

"There's a reason," Alexis said, with more confidence than she had. "I think it's, like, an energy thing. Down is calm, or."

Carina looked at her the way she looked at wrong answers in calculus. "You're making that up."

"Fine. It's toward the audience, that's what matters, move." But it ate at her for the rest of the scene, the way a wrong answer on a quiz eats at you after you've handed it in. She was the director. She was supposed to know why the words in her own mouth meant what they meant.

The rehearsal stumbled along. Carina delivered her big monologue while Jeffrey stood petulant in the corner with his arms crossed because Alexis had cut one of his lines, and when Alexis asked him to project, he said, "I'm projecting, you're standing too far away," which was technically true and completely unhelpful. She reset the scene twice, then a third time, and felt the whole evening tilting toward the kind of chaos that only pretending to be organized can produce. What she wanted, and wanted badly, was for the room to hold still while she figured out how to shape it.

At nine, Mr. Wijaya from next door knocked gently on the door frame, having let himself halfway in. He was holding a book, cloth-bound, older than Alexis. "I could hear you through the wall," he said. "My hearing aids are turned toward theatre, apparently." He held out the book. "It was my brother's. Stagecraft. Take it."

After he left, she looked up from the index, and there it was, plain as anything. She read the page twice. Then she called the actors back to the tape.

"Okay. Upstage is away from the audience and downstage is toward it," she said, and before Jeffrey could open his mouth she went on, "the terms come from old raked stages that sloped down toward the audience. So downstage was literally downhill." She could feel the shape of the thing in her head now, the whole tilted floor of it, actors trudging upward to the back, drifting down toward the crowd. "It's called a raked stage."

Jeffrey chewed on this. "So every flat stage is a ruin of a slope."

"Sure," Alexis said. "Everything is a ruin of something."

They ran the scene again with that in her mind, and it changed things in a way she couldn't fully defend. She stopped thinking of the room as flat. When Carina retreated upstage during the argument with Jeffrey, Alexis let her go farther than the tape said, all the way to the kitchen doorway, because distance from the audience read as withdrawal, and Carina's character was a person withdrawing. When Jeffrey came downstage to plead, she brought him almost to the carpet's edge. The room began to feel like it had a grade to it, a slope of attention running downhill toward the invisible audience, and the scene's temperature dropped and rose in a rhythm that finally resembled weather.

She did not know yet whether the play would be good. That stayed uncertain, the way most things did once she stopped pretending otherwise; Carina still rushed the monologue, Jeffrey still fought her on the cut line, and her mother would want the coffee table back by Sunday. But when they ran the whole first act, and Carina stood at the top of the room with her back half-turned, and Jeffrey came down toward the light of the television that was standing in for everything, Alexis sat very still on the arm of the couch and thought, not yet, not yet, don't stop yet.

"Keep going," she said.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The hardware store on Fram Street kept a deli counter at the back, three glass cases of shaved ham and provolone, because in a town of two thousand you sold whatever walked in the door. Abigail had walked in for wing nuts and walked out with an application, which she filled out at the register while the owner rang up a coil of clothesline for the man ahead of her. He glanced at her birthdate, said seventeen worked fine for stocking and registers, and asked if she could start Saturday. She said yes before she had fully decided to, which was becoming a pattern her mother called enthusiasm and her friend Terrence called a red flag.

Saturday morning he handed her an apron still warm from the dryer and a laminated sheet titled OPENING TASKS. Most of it was ordinary. Sweep the aisles facing the window, restock the paint rollers, wipe down the deli cases with the sanitizer under the sink. She liked the work more than she had expected to. There was a logic to the store, a taxonomy of need, and she found herself wondering how a person decided to stock sixty kinds of screws and only one kind of doormat, what combination of habit and accident had come to underwrite the whole arrangement.

At eleven the owner's wife went to pick up their son from soccer, and the owner got a phone call about a bulk order of fencing, and for a moment Abigail was alone near the deli. A man in a paint-spattered cap leaned over the counter and asked for a half pound of roast turkey, thin sliced. Behind the cases stood the slicer, chrome and gleaming, a machine she had watched the wife operate all morning with the easy boredom of someone doing a task that no longer required thought.

"Sure," Abigail said, and reached for the handle of the case.
