Then she stopped. Somewhere in the packet of papers she had signed was a page about labor laws, and she remembered a line from it, one she had skimmed the way she skimmed everything at seventeen. She had assumed it was about forklifts or ladders. But the phrase had stayed with her, and now it surfaced whole: under US federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant. She turned the words over. Even in a grocery store deli. The law had anticipated this exact room, this exact machine, this exact neophyte in an apron.

"I can't do the slicing," she said. "I'm seventeen, and workers under eighteen aren't allowed to operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant." She heard how it sounded, like a pamphlet, and felt her face go warm.

The man looked at her for a long second, and she could not read whether he was annoyed or amused or simply recalculating his lunch. "Well," he said. "That's a specific thing to know."

"I read it this morning. I wasn't sure it applied here."

"Kid," he said, "everything applies here eventually."

The owner came off the phone mid-sentence about fence posts, took in the scene with one glance, and apologized to the man, who waved it off and asked instead for whatever turkey was already sliced. Abigail stood with her hands at her sides while the owner worked the machine, and she was careful not to look like she was watching, though she was watching everything, the guard, the thickness dial, the way he shut it down and locked the blade before wiping it. When the man left with his bag, the owner turned to her.

"You could've just sliced it," he said. Not angry. Testing, maybe, or curious in the flat way adults were curious about teenagers who quoted federal regulations at them.

"I don't think I could've," she said. "I mean legally. That part I'm sure of." She hesitated, because the rest was less sure, and she found she wanted to say the true version rather than the confident one. "Whether I should have said something right then, or gotten you first, I don't know. It felt like both were wrong in different ways."

He nodded slowly, the way he had nodded at her application. "The disaffected kid my nephew sent me last summer wouldn't have said anything at all. Would've sliced it, cut himself, and said nothing." He handed her the sanitizer rag. "Cases. Then registers at noon, if you want them."

She took the rag. Behind the glass, the slicer sat with its blade locked, catching the light from the front window in a thin bright line, and she thought she would like to learn it, someday, at eighteen, the way the wife had learned it, easy and bored. She wiped down the cases and watched the parking lot for the next customer.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Each transfer RNA carries one amino acid and has a three-base anticodon that pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA.
story:
The trail behind the school cut through a strip of woods too thin to get lost in, which was the point, because Ms. Pritchard had decided the biology class would rehearse its exam answers out here where nobody could overhear them being wrong. Anais walked between Sage and Hugo, carrying a shoebox of index cards that the teacher had prepared the night before. Each card bore a three-letter code on one side and a word like "phenylalanine" or "leucine" on the other, and Anais had spent the walk trying to guess what the words meant.

"Okay," Ms. Pritchard said when they reached the clearing where a fallen oak made a natural bench. "Hugo, you're the ribosome. Stand there and don't move. Sage, you're the messenger RNA. Unzip your jacket and hold it open like a line, and Anais, take the box. You're all of the transfer RNAs at once."

"That's biologically inaccurate," Hugo said, planting himself on the log with the satisfaction of someone who has been told to do nothing.

"So is my salary. Anais, read the first card."

Anais turned the top card over. On the codon side it said AAA, and on the other side, in Ms. Pritchard's round handwriting, phenylalanine. Sage was already holding her jacket stretched out, having written a sequence of three-base codes up and down the lining in marker at the teacher's instruction that morning. The first one, near Sage's collar, read UUU.

"I don't know what to do," Anais said.

"Match them," said Hugo, from the log. "Look for the one that fits."

She looked. The card in her hand said AAA and the jacket said UUU, and she thought of the homework problem she'd gotten wrong two nights ago, the one that had started all this, where she'd written that the tRNA carried the codon instead of the anticodon. She hadn't understood the difference until she'd had to redo it, and even then the redoing felt like copying rather than knowing. Now she held the card up beside the jacket lining, AAA against UUU, and the fit was so plainly visible that she laughed.

"It's like a key," she said. "Each one of these cards carries one amino acid, that word on the back, and the three letters on the front are the anticodon, and it pairs with the matching codon on the messenger RNA. That's what makes it line up right." She pressed the card to the spot below Sage's collar. "Phenalanine. Phenylalanine, sorry."

"Next," said Ms. Pritchard, and Anais drew the next card, and the next, walking slowly down the length of Sage's jacket like someone reading a wall. Some cards matched and some didn't, and the ones that didn't she set aside in a small obdurate pile, cards that refused to pair no matter how she turned them, and Ms. Pritchard said, "Good, notice that, notice that some of them just don't fit, and think about what that tells you."

By the time they reached the hem of the jacket Anais had laid eleven cards in order down Sage's arm, each with its word facing out, and Ms. Pritchard asked her what the words spelled when you read them in sequence.

"A protein," Anais said. "The order of the amino acids is the protein. The order comes from the order of the codons, which comes from, I guess, the DNA, which I still don't fully have. I can get from here back to the DNA but the copying part, the transcription, I have it as a picture in my head and not as words yet."

"That's an honest answer," said Ms. Pritchard. "Better than a fluent one."

Hugo had been quiet, which for Hugo was suspicious, and when Anais glanced over he was frowning at the row of cards. "It bothers me," he said. "It's all this machinery and none of it knows anything. The cards don't know they're spelling a protein. Does that ever bother you, Anais? It's like the opposite of meaning. Little blind pieces lining up and the lining up is you."

"That's not nihilism," Sage said, from inside her jacket. "That's just chemistry. Nihilism is when you decide it means nothing. This is when it means something without deciding."

"Those aren't different enough for me yet," Anais said, and found, saying it, that she meant it as a question rather than a position. She looked at the card still in her hand, the one that had refused to pair, CCG against no matching spot on the jacket, its word glycine facing up at the canopy. Somewhere in her own cells, right now, a version of this was happening, some piece of her matching itself against some other piece of her, and none of it deciding anything, and her standing here on a trail understanding a corner of it. She wondered whether understanding catalyzed anything, or whether it was just another card finding its spot.

She put the unpaired card in her pocket instead of back in the box. "Can we run it again," she said, "from the collar down, and this time I want to be the messenger RNA."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
The envelope sat on the kitchen table between the fruit bowl and Laura's chemistry homework, and she had been circling it for two days the way a cat circles a recalcitrant moth. It was her first credit card statement. She had gotten the card in September, mostly because the forms had been there at the freshman orientation fair with free pens, and she had used it exactly four times: a bus pass, a textbook the used-copy hadn't covered, a birthday present for her mother, and sandwiches for herself and Mary the night they stayed late building the physics project.

Now the statement said she owed one hundred and twelve dollars, and at the bottom, in a box that seemed designed to be friendly, it said her minimum payment was twenty-five dollars. Twenty-five was practically nothing. Twenty-five she could pay out of her babysitting money tonight and still have enough left for the movies. One hundred and twelve was her whole savings envelope, the one taped inside her desk drawer that she had been growing since eighth grade.

Mary came over after cross-country practice, smelling of rain and borrowed deodorant, and dropped her bag on the chair opposite. She had a vocabulary quiz Monday and spread her list across the table, chewing the cap of a pen. "Consanguinity," she read. "Consanguinity. Why do I need to know about blood relations for English." Laura slid the statement across to her without saying anything, the way you hand someone a spider to identify.

"You have a credit card?"

"Two months. And now this."

Mary turned the page over, squinted at the fine print like it was written in a language she almost knew. "What are you going to do, the twenty-five?"

That was the question. Laura took the page back and read the box again, slower this time. The word minimum was doing something interesting, she thought; it wasn't saying recommended or sensible, it was saying least, the floor. Below it, in smaller type, was a sentence about a grace period, and she read it twice because the first time she didn't believe it. If she paid the full balance by the due date, she would owe no interest on her purchases at all. None. The card would have lent her the money for a month and charged her nothing.

"Wait," she said out loud. "So the sandwiches, the bus pass, all of it, if I pay the whole hundred and twelve by the due date, there's no interest. It's like a free loan."

"Then why does the twenty-five exist?"

Laura turned the paper sideways, as though the answer might be hiding in the layout. If she paid only twenty-five, the sentence seemed to say, the grace period would not apply; interest would begin to be charged, would go on being charged, month after month, on money she had already spent. The minimum was not a mercy. It was a doorway into a room you paid rent for.

She got the envelope from her drawer and counted it onto the table next to Mary's vocabulary list, which had consanguinity staring up between a ten and a five. The whole bill took most of it. Her savings, which she had watched grow from coins to bills over three years, would shrink back to almost nothing, and something in her resisted that, the same part of her that hated emptying a jar. But the money wasn't really gone, she reasoned; it was going to the card now instead of later, and later was when the card got expensive. Growing money and borrowing money seemed almost like the same machine running in two directions; every month you waited, the same percentage either lifted you or leaned on you. She tried to subsume both of them under one idea, interest as time having a price, and it almost held, though she couldn't have said whether it was truly one principle or two wearing the same coat.

Her father came home while she was filling out the check, shaking rain off his jacket, and asked what the pile of money on the table was for.

"Being poor later so I'm not poorer after that," Laura said.

He looked at her for a moment, then at the statement, and she watched him decide not to turn it into a lecture, for which she loved him. He only put the kettle on.

Mary copied consanguinity onto a fresh page, saying it under her breath like an incantation. "You know it's not really like family," she said, tapping the card. "You and the bank."

"Obviously not."

"I'm just saying. Family you're stuck with whether you pay or not."

Laura wrote the check for one hundred and twelve dollars, signed it, and put it in the return envelope with the little plastic window, thinking that she would rebuild the envelope in the drawer, that next month she would pay in full again, and that she still wasn't entirely sure which was wiser, keeping the card for its free month of borrowing or cutting it up before it found some new way to be recalcitrant. She licked the envelope, pressed it flat, and set it on top of her keys for the morning.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes.
story:
The elevator in the old building smelled of cabbage and floor wax, and Aaron rode it down with his mother, who was holding a folder of papers against her chest the way other people held babies. They were moving out of the apartment on the fourth floor, the one with the radiator that clanked all winter, and today was the day of the open house Ms. Ong was holding two streets over for her basement suite. Aaron had spent the morning photographing the walls.

He had started doing it the night before, after the landlord's letter about the deposit. His dad had read it aloud at dinner: deductions for the marks on the walls, the scuffs on the baseboards, the small holes where Aaron had hung his chemistry posters in grade nine. His mother had said something bitter about landlords and solvency always mattering more than tenants, and then the conversation had gone somewhere Aaron couldn't follow, so he had gone to his room with his phone. He didn't know what he was looking for until he found it, on a tenants' rights page that a girl named Rebecca from his civics class had shared back in September. A security deposit is held to cover unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear, so in many jurisdictions a landlord cannot deduct for ordinary aging like small nail holes. He read it three times. Then he walked the apartment with the phone up, shooting every wall, every corner, every nail hole, the kitchen tap that dripped, the closet door that had never quite closed since the building settled. He photographed the small holes where the posters had been, zooming in until they were grey craters against white.

At the open house, the basement suite was brighter than he expected. Ms. Ong, small and quick, had set out a plate of mandarin slices on the counter, and a few strangers drifted through touching the countertops. Gianluca had come along because his own family needed a place by June, and he stood in the kitchen asking Ms. Ong about heat included or not, his voice going formal the way it did around adults. His family had been in a motel since the fire, Aaron knew, and Gianluca had said, once, on the bus, that if this place worked his mother would stop sleeping in her coat.

"See anything you like?" Ms. Ong asked Aaron, catching him in the smaller bedroom.

"It's good," Aaron said. "We live two streets over. We're moving out of our place."

"Ah." She straightened a curtain. "Then you know the drill. Deposit, first month, references. My last tenants, lovely people, but the walls." She ran a thumb along a scuff near the door frame. "I had to keep part of the deposit for that."

Aaron felt the page from last night assemble itself in his head. "Can you, though?" he asked. "For scuffs?"

She looked at him. "It's a security deposit. It covers damage."

"Beyond normal wear and tear," Aaron said. "That's what it's held for. Unpaid rent or damage past ordinary aging. Like small nail holes. In a lot of jurisdictions the landlord can't deduct for that. Ordinary aging, I mean." He was aware of Gianluca listening from the doorway, and of his own pulse, because Ms. Ong might tell him he was wrong.

She was quiet for a moment, peeling a mandarin. "My last place before this one," she said finally. "When I was the tenant, my landlord kept two hundred dollars for the state of the walls. I didn't know enough to argue. Then I became the landlord and I did the same thing, because I thought that was just how it went." She ate a segment. "Where did you learn that?"

"Photographed my walls last night," Aaron said. "All of them. Every nail hole."

"Smart boy," she said, not warmly, but like she was filing it away. In the main room his mother was signing a form on the counter, the pen moving fast, and the old boiler in the corner made its obsolescent clank, the same dead rhythm as the one at home, and Aaron found that strangely steadying, like the building itself admitting what it was.

Gianluca drifted over as the strangers thinned out. "Is it true, though?" he asked quietly. "What you said. Because if my mom gets a place, they're going to do the same thing to us."

"It's true for a lot of places," Aaron said. "I don't know if it's true here. That's the part I have to check." He was honest about that, at least to himself: the page had said many jurisdictions, not all, and he didn't yet know which kind they lived in. But he had forty-one photographs on his phone, and a landlord's letter, and Rebecca, who had shared the page in the first place and would probably know where to look next.

Ms. Ong came back from showing someone out. She looked at Aaron's mother's signature drying on the form, then at Aaron. "Bring the photos when you move in," she said. "We'll take some together. Both of us, same walls. Then nobody argues later."

"I'll bring my phone," Aaron said, and held it up, the camera already open.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, usually a prime minister, holds office by keeping the confidence of the legislature rather than by winning a separate popular election.
story:
The metal detector at the courthouse swallowed Oakley's granola bar, or rather the security guard did, holding it up to the light like evidence and then pocketing it with the solemnity of a man impounding contraband. Behind them, Ms. Popescu counted heads for the third time, which was her congenital response to field trips, as though any student left behind would be her personal burden until the end of time. Liam tugged at the tie his father had knotted for him in the driveway, too tight, and followed Youssef through the glass doors into a lobby that smelled of floor wax and old paper.

They had come for a hearing, though the case itself was modest: a citizens' group appealing a municipal decision, an argument about signatures and deadlines that would never make the news. The real assignment was Ms. Popescu's. Each of them had to observe how a public proceeding actually worked and then, that evening, submit a page comparing it to how a country chooses and removes its head of government, since the unit had gone by in a blur of diagrams she'd drawn on the board while half the class slept. Liam had not slept, exactly, but he had absorbed the diagrams the way one absorbs wallpaper.

His father, meanwhile, had firm opinions. Over breakfast he had talked about a petition circulating online, the kind that demanded the people be allowed to vote the prime minister out directly, and he'd told Liam to keep his eyes open at the courthouse because this was how real accountability started, in rooms like this one, with citizens standing up. Liam had promised nothing, but he'd written in his notebook, in his father's borrowed certainty, that the prime minister owed his job to the voters, full stop, the same way a president does, and that anything else was a trick played by insiders.

The courtroom was smaller than television had prepared him for, wood-paneled and humid, with a judge who looked as though the proceedings had failed to enrapture him since roughly 1994. The citizens' group lost on a technicality within forty minutes, which struck Liam as both anticlimactic and, in some way he couldn't yet name, more interesting than winning would have been. Where did a person go, he wondered, when the room itself decided against them? Was there a bigger room somewhere, or did the decision just die on the floor?

Oakley elbowed him during the recess. "Your notebook says the PM got voted in by the people. Like a president."

"Everyone knows that," Liam said.

Youssef, who had spent the drive explaining that his grandmother never stopped arguing about politics, shook his head slowly, almost gently, the way one corrects a friend who has been confidently wrong in front of strangers. "Nobody voted directly for the prime minister. He keeps the office by holding the confidence of the legislature, not by winning a separate popular election." He said it flatly, without drama, and then went back to his notes, leaving the sentence sitting on the bench between them like a dropped glove.

Liam sat with it. So the prime minister stood or fell not by the ballot that had elected him, but by whether the legislature still tolerated him, which meant the same voters could hand a party a victory and then, through their representatives, pull the whole leader down mid-term. Whereas a president served out the term unless something extraordinary happened, removable by a process that was deliberately hard. Two ways of arranging the same longing, he thought, the way carbon arranges itself into graphite or diamond, allotropes of the same element: one soft and swift, one hard and slow, and neither obviously the true form. His father's petition assumed a directness that had never existed. He underlined his breakfast certainty, drew a line through it, and felt something between embarrassment and relief.

The twist came in the hallway, when the citizens' group's lawyer stopped to shake Ms. Popescu's hand and recognized Liam, of all people, from the local paper's photo of a model parliament he'd attended in grade eleven. "You're the one who argued the government should fall," she said cheerfully. "You were good." Liam laughed, because he had, and because he had spent that whole weekend believing the prime minister was simply elected like a president, and nobody had corrected him, and he had still won best delegate. Maybe, he thought, you can be right in a room and wrong in a country.

On the bus he started his page twice, tore nothing up, and left both versions. He wrote that he now preferred the parliamentary answer to removal, because a government that could fall when it lost the room's confidence seemed more honest than one that waited out a clock, but that he couldn't decide whether choosing a leader through that same confidence was protection or slight of hand, and he wasn't going to pretend the page settled it. Oakley leaned over the seat and read the last line upside down, then asked, "So if you called your dad tonight, what would you tell him?" Liam looked out the window at the courthouse steps shrinking behind them, and said, "I'd tell him the petition needs a rewrite."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
The market opened at eight, and by ten the canvas awnings were snapping in a wind that came down off the ridge in slow, visible waves, making the whole row of stalls undulate like something alive. Paige walked the aisle with a canvas bag and a list her mother had written in the car: onions, a chicken, something green. It was her turn to cook the Sunday meal, a bargain struck in June before her brother left for his internship, and she had promised to do it properly, at the campsite, over the little two-burner stove.

Jasper was working the cheese table for his uncle, and he leaned on the crate when he saw her. "Still doing the big dinner," he said. It wasn't a question. He'd been at the lake with her family last August, the weekend she'd boiled the potatoes for forty minutes and served them with a fork that bounced off the centers. He'd eaten them anyway, out of politeness or stubbornness, and said nothing until everyone else had noticed too.

"Last time was a disaster," Paige said. "I set the timer the way I always do at home. Twenty minutes. The pasta came out like wire."

Edmond appeared from behind the honey jars, where he'd been arguing with a customer about wildflower versus clover. "That happened to my grandmother," he said. "She moved to the mountains and her beans took all day. She thought her pot was broken." He wiped his hands on his apron. "Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about ninety-five degrees Celsius at five thousand feet. So boiled foods take longer to cook. You just have to give them more time."

"Nobody told me that in physics," Paige said.

"Nobody told me either. My grandmother told me, and I thought she was making it up until I looked it up."

She bought the chicken, the onions, a bundle of chard whose stems she snapped to test, and a bag of small yellow potatoes because her mother had asked for them even after last summer. At the far end of the row, Ms. Perera from the chemistry department was choosing peppers with great deliberation, holding each one to the light. Paige hesitated, then went over. "Is it true about water up here?" she asked. "That it boils lower?"

Ms. Perera looked pleased, the way she did when a student asked something outside the syllabus. "At this elevation, close enough to ninety-five degrees," she said. "A watched pot boils early and cooks late, up here. That's not the saying, but it should be." She put a pepper in her basket and moved on, and Paige stood for a moment holding her bag, a little annoyed at herself for needing the confirmation.

The campsite sat at the edge of a meadow, and by late afternoon the wind had come up again, flattening the grass in long silver stripes. Paige filled the big pot from the water jug and set it on the burner while her father gathered wood and her mother read in the car with the door open. This time she had a plan: potatoes in first, a full half hour before the pasta, and she wrote the times on the back of the shopping list in pencil, then crossed them out and rewrote them later.

The water, when it finally boiled, was not the rolling fury she knew from her grandmother's kitchen at sea level. It murmured and shivered, and when she dropped the pasta in it went quiet for a long moment, as though the water were reconsidering. She had wanted to think of herself as someone who had been simply unlucky before, a victim of a bad stove or a bad clock, but standing there stirring, she understood it was more like having been fluent in a language that meant something different four thousand feet higher. Jasper's silence that night last August, which she had taken for kindness, might also have been a kind of circumlocution, his way of not saying what they both could see: that she had cooked with total confidence in the wrong world.

She lifted a potato out at twenty-eight minutes and cut it open, and it was floury all the way through, no glassy ring at the center. The chicken browned in the cast iron pan while the chard wilted in the last of the water, which had gone turbid with starch, clouded and faintly white, and she poured a cup of it over the pasta bowl the way her grandmother did. They ate at the folding table with the light going long and amber across the meadow, and her mother said, "This is the best thing you've made," and her father said nothing with his mouth full, which was his highest praise.

Later, washing up at the spigot in the dark, Paige found one potato left in the bottom of the pot, under the water, still firm. She fished it out and held it under the cold tap, turning it in her fingers. She could call Jasper tomorrow and tell him it worked. Or she could bring the potato to school on Monday, hard as a pebble, and set it on Edmond's honey table without a word, and see how long it took him to laugh.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In the United States, a conventional mortgage with a down payment below 20 percent usually requires private mortgage insurance, which protects the lender, not the buyer.
story:
Mason had been carrying the same two numbers in his head for three weeks: four thousand dollars, which was what he had saved from the garden center, and six hundred fifty, which was what a room cost in Henri's building if one came open. So when Henri texted that his older cousin Devon had finally closed on a condo across the hall, Mason took the bus over with his bank app already open, as if the numbers might behave differently in someone else's apartment.

The place smelled like the champagne somebody had spilled at the closing party and nobody had fully mopped. Lily-Rose was there, sitting cross-legged on the kitchen counter, eating the last of the cheese while Henri hunted for a corkscrew that had already migrated to the living room. On the table lay a folder from the lender, thick as a phone book, and on top of it a single page titled Monthly Payment Breakdown. Mason picked it up because he wanted to see what six hundred fifty a month looked like on paper, in official font.

The page had more lines than he expected. Principal. Interest. Taxes. And then, near the bottom, a smaller line labeled PMI, eighty-one dollars, with nothing beside it explaining what the letters stood for. He read it twice, then held the page up toward the kitchen. "Henri, what's PMI?"

Henri's grandmother was still there from the party, wrapped in a cardigan against the air conditioning, and she answered before Henri could. "Private mortgage insurance," she said. "Devon put ten percent down, so he has to carry it." She tapped her own temple. "And you want to remember it protects the lender, not him. He pays every month and gets nothing from it."

"Then why agree to it?" Mason asked.

"Because nobody his age has twenty percent of a condo in the bank." She said it kindly, the way she said most things, and went back to her cold tea.

Lily-Rose slid off the counter and came to look over Mason's shoulder, which he had been half hoping she would. "What's ten percent of this place?" she asked. He found the purchase price on the first page and did the arithmetic against his thumb. The down payment was more than four times his savings, and that was before the closing costs the breakdown listed underneath, which he had not known were a thing. Rent, by contrast, wanted only first month, last month, and a security deposit, which the landlord held but technically did not keep. It felt almost gentle by comparison.

He had come wanting to externalize the decision, to get it out of his head and onto a table where other people could poke at it, and it was working, though not in the direction he had assumed. He had thought the question was whether he could afford to stop renting, and now the question seemed to be whether renting was a trap or a rung. Lily-Rose argued the rung side with real conviction: flexibility, no repairs, deposit back at the end. Henri, drying champagne flutes, argued the trap side by pointing at his own ceiling, where a water stain had been there since February because the landlord could take his time. Ms. Rahimi, who lived one floor down and had come up to return a borrowed roasting pan, stood in the doorway listening with her coat still on. "Both of you are right," she offered, "which is the most annoying thing about money."

By the time the evening thinned out, Mason had reached something he would have called a detente rather than an answer: renting was what his savings actually supported, and buying was a real thing that existed for a later version of him, and the honest part was admitting he could not yet see the line between the two. He told Lily-Rose so in the hallway, quietly, while Henri argued with his grandmother about who was taking the roasting pan down. Lily-Rose considered it, chewing the last corner of cheese.

"There's a room opening on the third floor in March," she said. "Ms. Rahimi's building. I heard her tell Henri's grandmother while you were staring at that page."

"Six fifty?"

"Seven twenty. She said the landlord raised it, because with the new buyer across the street, everything around here is going up."

Mason laughed once, not because it was funny. He had spent the whole evening learning that Devon paid eighty-one dollars a month for insurance that protected somebody else, and now he understood he had been paying the same kind of money all along, only nobody had printed it on a page for him. He put the lender's breakdown back on the table, square with the edge, the way Devon would want it.

"Tell Ms. Rahimi I'll come look at the room," he said. "I'd like to meet the landlord I'm already insuring."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
The loan officer's desk had a bowl of lollipops and a pamphlet stand, and Natalie took one of each because refusing free things in a bank felt like leaving money on the table. Her mother had asked her along to look at refinancing offers, mostly to hold the folder, but partly, Natalie suspected, because her mother enjoyed telling strangers that her daughter was "good with numbers." The officer, whose desk plate read Mr. Horváth, slid two printouts across the table. The first was from 2021, a rate so low it looked like a typo. The second was this week's.

"Okay," Natalie said, "why is this one almost four times that one? What happened?"

Mr. Horváth smiled the way adults smile when they're about to say ask your teacher. "The Federal Reserve raised rates. Started in March of 2022, from basically zero, and kept going until July of 2023, when they got to a range of five and a quarter to five and a half percent."

Her mother frowned at the papers as though they had personally insulted her. "But why would they do that to people?"

Natalie chewed her lollipop and thought about her economics homework, which she had been avoiding by alphabetizing her sock drawer. She knew the pieces, sort of, the way she knew the words to songs she couldn't sing. "It's the inflation thing," she said slowly. "Prices were going up too fast. So the Fed raises the rate, and then borrowing costs more, so people buy fewer big things, houses, cars, business equipment, and when people stop fighting over stuff, prices calm down." She heard herself say it and waited to be corrected.

"You'll get an A," Mr. Horváth said. "Or a job here."

"Not both?" her mother said. "She needs a fallback."

While her mother and Mr. Horváth discussed points and fees, Natalie texted Deven, who was in the same econ class and had opinions about everything, including, once, an eleven-paragraph analysis of cafeteria gravy. She typed: at bank with mom. mortgage stuff. just explained rate hikes to a grown man and he didn't laugh. Deven replied with a video of a cat falling off a counter, then: explain it to me then. no googling.

She leaned against the pamphlet stand. The trouble was that in class she'd learned it as a diagram, arrows on the board, and diagrams were useless in a bank where an actual person was about to pay an actual extra several hundred a month. She typed: think of it like traffic. everyone driving at once means everyone honks and prices go up. the fed raises the toll. fewer people drive. less honking. Deven sent back: that's terrible. honks are inflation? She wrote: yes. honks are inflation. He wrote: then say it better.

She was still glaring at her phone when Mr. Horváth finished with her mother and turned to her. "Studying this in school?"

"Trying to," she said. "The part I can't figure out is who the Fed actually feels bad for. Because the high rate helps people who saved money, their savings earn more, but it hurts people who need to borrow. My mom's in the second group." She glanced over. "So is that fair or not?"

He rocked his chair back. "That's a question for economists, and they argue about it over drinks."

"That's not an answer."

"No," he agreed. "It's a reason to keep asking."

In the car, her mother hummed along to the radio, and Natalie realized she had gone into the bank thinking the whole thing was one machine, that there was a right answer somewhere that adults kept in a drawer, and now she understood it was more like two true things pressing on each other. Saving rewarded, borrowing punished, and the lever in between moved both. She texted Deven one more time: fine. the toll isn't fair or unfair. it's a trade. also i now know what a basis point is and you don't. He answered: TRUCE. amnesty for the honk theory. She wrote: never. the honk theory is eternal.

At home she found her mother at the kitchen table with the printouts fanned out like losing lottery tickets, and her mother said, "So, smart one. Do we wait or do we take the worse rate now?"

Natalie sat down across from her. Outside, a neighbor's sprinkler extruded its thin silver arc over the lawn, patient and absurd in the heat. "I can explain why the rate is what it is," she said. "I can't tell you what it'll be next year. Nobody can. Not even Mr. Horváth, and he had a whole bowl of lollipops."

Her mother tapped the 2021 printout with one finger. "So your genius economics has limits."

"Phenotypic limits," Natalie said, before she could stop herself, because Deven had spent a week using the word for every kind of visible shortcoming, and it had migrated into her mouth like a stowaway. "It means you can see them."

"I can see the bills too," her mother said, and pulled the calculator toward her. "Show me the difference again. Slowly this time."

Natalie slid her chair around and started with March 2022.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
Laura had the whole table by the window, which was the only good thing about a Sunday. Three books on the Court of late nineteenth century, her laptop, a legal pad covered in crossed-out sentences, and, pinned under her elbow, the draft Ms. Suzuki had handed back on Friday with a single note in green pen across the top. The paper was due Tuesday at eight in the morning, and the note said: "This is a fact, not a thesis. What are you actually arguing? See me."

The draft's first paragraph, the one she'd been proud of, ended with the sentence she'd typed at one in the morning: The Supreme Court's decision in Plessy v. Ferguson upheld racial segregation in public facilities for decades. Ms. Suzuki had underlined it twice. Laura read the underline as acerbic, though it was probably just habit. Under it, in smaller letters: "Who disputes this?"

Lilly slid into the chair across from her with an iced coffee she wasn't supposed to have in the library and read the note upside down. "She's saying it's wrong?"

"She's saying it's true." Laura turned the paper right side up, as if that would help. "That's the problem. It's true and everyone knows it. She circled a sentence in the margin here, some question about how a reasonable person could argue with me, and I don't know what that means. If nobody could argue with it, isn't that good?"

"You wrote eight pages," Lilly said. "You have footnotes. I saw you making the footnotes at two in the morning."

"The footnotes are fine. The footnotes are beautiful." Laura opened her laptop and showed her: the Chicago style sheet Ms. Suzuki had given them in September, the indentation exactly right, the bibliography alphabetized, every superscript number in order. "I learned all of that. I can cite a court case, a newspaper article, a scholarly journal. That part I can do in my sleep now. It's the sentence the citations are supposed to serve that's broken."

Lilly sucked the last of her coffee through the straw, thinking. "So what's the paper actually about? Like, what do you think about it?"

That was the question, and Laura had been avoiding it for two weeks because answering it felt presumptuous. She'd read the dissents, the historians, the dissenting historians. Somewhere in her notes there was a half-sentence she'd written and never developed: that the decision did something worse than permit segregation, that it gave segregation a legal vocabulary that outlived the ruling itself. She found it on the legal pad, halfway down a page, circled it, and felt something in her plan for the evening quietly destabilize, the whole outline she'd built tipping toward a paper she hadn't researched yet.

Kalan texted at four, and Laura held the phone where Lilly could see it. "Is ur thesis fixed? Mine was a fact too, she wrote WHO DISPUTES on it in green, whole study group panicked, we're at the diner if u want." Lilly read it aloud in a flat voice and then said, "The whole study group. That's twenty kids all discovering at once that they've been summarizing instead of arguing." Laura typed back a reply, deleting it twice before she sent it: "Mine's a mess. A reasonable person could dispute what I'm writing now. That's apparently the point. Wish me luck." Then she put the phone face down and pulled the stack of books closer.

By six she had a new thesis on the pad, written out slowly so she couldn't fool herself with speed: Plessy did not simply permit segregation; it legitimized it, transforming local custom into constitutional doctrine and thereby making segregation harder to dismantle than it would have been under a ruling that struck it down. She looked at it and understood, for the first time, the difference between knowing a chain of events and staking a claim on their meaning. It was like epistemology had been a word in a textbook and was suddenly a thing she was doing, standing on evidence she chose and defending ground that someone else could stand on differently. A reasonable person could read the same documents she'd read and say the ruling changed less than she claimed, that custom had already hardened, that the Court followed rather than led. She could already hear that person. She wrote a sentence in the margin acknowledging it, because pretending there was no other side felt like a smaller, sneakier version of the original mistake.

At closing time she was on her last footnote, checking the page numbers against the bibliography while the lights above the stacks clicked off in sections. Ms. Suzuki came around the reference desk with her coat on and her keys out, and stopped at the window table long enough to read the new first paragraph over Laura's shoulder. She didn't say anything for a moment, and Laura kept her eyes on the screen, her hand still on the pen.

"Somebody could fight you on that," Ms. Suzuki said.

"I know," Laura said. "I left them the opening. Page nine."
